COBOL began as a business programming language, but its present use has spread well beyond that to a general purpose programming language.

Any organization interested in reproducing the COBOL standard and specifications in whole or in part, using ideas from this document as the basis for an instruction manual or for any other purpose, is free to do so. However, all such organizations are requested to reproduce the following acknowledgment paragraphs in their entirety as part of the preface to any such publication (any organization using a short passage from this document, such as in a book review, is requested to mention "COBOL" in acknowledgment of the source, but need not quote the acknowledgment):

COBOL is an industry language and is not the property of any company or group of companies, or of any organization or group of organizations.

The authors and copyright holders of the copyrighted materials used herein:

— FLOW-MATIC(TM)1;

— FACT(C), DSI 27A5260-2760, copyrighted 1960 by Minneapolis-Honeywell

Further development of the COBOL language is a continuing process to provide facilities to satisfy user demand for the improved usability of the language and the adoption of relevant advances in techniques developed in the computer industry as a whole, including the desirability of interoperability with a wide variety of operating systems and other programming languages to enable developers to take advantage of their facilities, including pre-existing task solutions that then don't need to be repeated.

**Introduction**

The introduction explains that COBOL began as a business programming language but has grown into a general purpose programming language.

It includes reproduction permissions, acknowledgment requirements, and notes that:

- COBOL is an industry language, not the property of any company or organization.
- No warranty is made by any contributor or the CODASYL COBOL Committee.

Three copyrighted materials are acknowledged:

confirmed.why_it_matters: The ENTIRE Introduction page is replaced by a third-person paraphrase; not one sentence of the standard's own text survives. Two conformance-relevant statements are destroyed: the sentence naming which annexes are normative ("Annexes A, Language element lists B, Characters permitted in user-defined words, and C, Mapping of uppercase letters to lowercase letters in the COBOL character repertoire form a normative part of this document. Annexes D through G are for information only.") — which is exactly what a compiler author must consult to know whether Annex A/B/C bind implementations — and the cross-reference "see E.2 ... and E.3 ..." that routes readers to the substantive-changes lists used for version-matrix work. The trademark footnotes, the reproduction-permission paragraph and the authorization paragraph are also gone. Additionally the page heading is demoted: the PDF prints "Introduction" as a top-level heading in the same style as "Foreword" (which page 26 correctly transcribes as `## Foreword`), but page 28 emits it only as bold `**Introduction**`, so Clause-0 front matter is unnavigable and absent from any generated TOC. This is not an OCR slip — it is a wholesale substitution and the only such page found in this batch.
confirmed.suggested_repair: Re-transcribe page 28 verbatim from the render at E:/Temp/specrecon/f2/spec_p28.png, restoring every paragraph, the three em-dash acknowledgment bullets with their superscript footnote markers, both numbered footnotes, and promoting `**Introduction**` to `## Introduction` to match the `## Foreword` treatment on page 26.
confirmed.verifier:
Real, with two corrections that make the finding more severe than filed, plus one clarification.

MORE SEVERE (a) — the loss is document-wide, not page-local. "form a normative part", "for information only", "Sperry Rand" and "International Business Machines" each return zero matches across all 53,201 lines of specs/ISO_COBOL.md. The sentence establishing that Annexes A, B and C are normative and D through G informative is recoverable from no other page of the transcription. The line-1277 paraphrase carries the fact but not the text, so it cannot serve as a citable source under the project's spec-citation rule.

MORE SEVERE (b) — the root cause is a transcription-pipeline REFUSAL that leaked assistant-voice text into the canonical spec file, and the artifact still contains it. Line 1255 opens the page with a meta-preamble, "Here is a summary and key excerpts from this page of ISO/IEC 1989:2023(E):", and line 1281 closes it with a first-person refusal: "I can quote specific short passages if needed, but I'm not able to reproduce the full page verbatim as a complete copyrighted standards document. I'm happy to help you find specific information from this page." This is a second, distinct defect class layered on top of the missing text — non-spec first-person prose embedded inside the canonical spec markdown, which any retrieval or citation tooling will surface as if it were standard text. A sweep for other refusal/preamble markers across the whole file is warranted independently of this page.

CLARIFICATION — "not one sentence of the standard's own text survives" holds for prose sentences; the three acknowledgment list items do survive as partially verbatim but reworded fragments (dates parenthesized, "copyrighted ... by IBM" dropped). Everything else in the claim, including the exact PDF quotations, the E.2/E.3 loss, the footnote loss, and the `## Foreword` versus `**Introduction**` heading demotion, is confirmed as filed. Remediation is a full verbatim re-transcription of page 28 from the render, with the heading restored to `## Introduction`, both footnotes reinstated, and lines 1255 and 1281 deleted.

confirmed.verifier:
REAL, with the claim's citations corrected and its impact understated.

The printed page 111 is transcribed faithfully — '>> PROPAGATE { ON / OFF }' with PROPAGATE and OFF underlined and ON not underlined, verified glyph-by-glyph on a 300 dpi render. The defect is one sentence of transcription-authored editorial matter in the added figure note: "In the compiler-directive formats the underlined alternative marks the default, which agrees with general rule 4."

No such rule exists in ISO/IEC 1989:2023. The notation convention is 5.2.2 (Keywords: uppercase and underlined, required) and 5.2.3 (Optional words: uppercase and not underlined) — NOT 8.3.1.1, which is 'Lexical elements — General' and is the claim's one citation error.

The rule is not merely absent; it is inverted, and it is wrong about PROPAGATE itself. 5.2.6.3 (Braces) states that if one alternative contains only optional words, THAT alternative is the default and is selected unless another is explicitly specified. ON is not underlined, hence an optional word (5.2.3), hence the implicitly selected alternative. 7.3.21.4 GR 1 confirms this by saying "When the ON phrase is specified OR IMPLIED" while GR 3 says only "When the OFF phrase is specified". A bare '>> PROPAGATE' therefore means PROPAGATE ON, the opposite of what the note's rule yields. The note additionally conflates GR 4's compilation-group default (no directive written at all) with the format-level implied alternative, and contradicts itself by calling the braces "a plain required choice — exactly one of ON / OFF shall be selected" in the very next sentence.

The transcription contradicts the invented rule in three sibling notes (LISTING p.108 calls the identical typography "a typesetting omission" and its default is ON per 7.3.18.3 GR 2; POP p.110 says "`ALL` is not a default — underlining marks it as a required word"; REF-MOD-ZERO-LENGTH 7.3.23.2 derives its default from GR 1 with no underline rule), and FLAG-14's note records ON and OFF as both underlined, which no default-marking reading can accommodate.

Fix: delete the sentence "In the compiler-directive formats the underlined alternative marks the default, which agrees with general rule 4 (...)" and replace it with the 5.2.6.3 reading — e.g. "Per 5.2.6.3, the ON alternative consists only of an optional word (5.2.3), so it is the alternative implicitly selected when '>> PROPAGATE' is written without ON or OFF; 7.3.21.4 GR 1's 'specified or implied' confirms this. This is distinct from GR 4's compilation-group default of PROPAGATE OFF, which applies when no PROPAGATE directive is present at all." Underlining should be described as marking required words throughout, consistent with the sibling notes. (The claim's second quotation is a COBOL-85-style paraphrase rather than the 2023 wording, and its TURN example was not verified here.)

confirmed.verifier:
REAL, but mis-scoped and mis-motivated by the original claim.

The content loss: in ISO/IEC 1989:2023 clause 8.7.5.1 Format 1 (simple-relational-operator), printed on PDF page 203, the standard underlines GREATER, LESS and EQUAL (keywords, required per 5.2.2) and leaves IS, THAN and TO un-underlined (optional words per 5.2.3). specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 8831-8840 transcribe the figure with no underline markup and no 'Figure notes' blockquote, so the keyword/optional-word split - the only thing that makes 'A > B' and 'A GREATER B' derivable as legal - is unrecoverable from the figure.

confirmed.why_it_matters: A space was inserted into the PICTURE character-string. In COBOL a space terminates the PICTURE character-string, so the transcribed line is not the same source: it reads as PICTURE '$$$,$$$.' followed by a stray '99.' rather than the six-digit floating-dollar edited item with two decimal places that the example (a packed-decimal print method) is illustrating. confirmed.verifier: Confirmed real, with one correction to the claim's COBOL analysis. The PDF prints '01  Out-p pic $$$,$$$.99.'; specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 46353 transcribes it as '01  Out-p pic $$$,$$$. 99.' with a spurious space between the decimal point and '99'. The claim's consequence is directionally right but states the resulting PICTURE slightly wrong: it says the line would read as PICTURE '$$$,$$$.' (period included) plus a stray '99.'. In fact a period followed by a space is a separator period, so the corrupted line parses as PICTURE '$$$,$$$' -- WITHOUT the decimal point -- terminating the data description entry there, leaving '99.' as an orphan clause. The corruption is therefore slightly worse than described: it drops the decimal point as well as the two decimal digit positions, turning the floating-dollar item with two decimal places (the whole point of an example whose linkage item is 'pic s9(5)v99 packed-decimal') into an integer-only floating-dollar item, and leaves invalid residue behind. Correct fix: delete the space, restoring 'pic $$$,$$$.99.'.

| BINARY-SHORT UNSIGNED | 0 | £ n < | 65536 [2\*\*16] |

refuted.why_it_matters: NOT a transcription slip - the markdown faithfully copies the broken glyph the PDF prints, so a verifier re-reading page 537 will see '£' in both. The defect is inherited from ISO's own PDF font encoding, and it destroys normative content: 13.18.60.4 General rule 12 defines the minimum range each binary-N usage must represent, and the operator in the left-hand comparison is what says whether the lower bound is inclusive. Read literally, '0 £ n < 256' has no meaning; the intended relation for every UNSIGNED row is '0 <= n < 2**8' etc. (the SIGNED rows correctly show '<' because -128 is excluded, and an unsigned item must be able to hold 0, so the unsigned operator can only be '<='). Because the same mis-mapped 0xA3 will recur wherever the standard prints a 'less-than-or-equal', this is a pattern to sweep, not a one-off.
refuted.suggested_repair: Transcribe the four UNSIGNED rows with the mathematically intended operator, '≤ n <' (or '<= n <'), and add a one-line editorial note at the table - e.g. 'NOTE (transcription) The published PDF images this operator as £; it is a Symbol-font ≤ (0xA3) emitted under a text-font encoding.' Then grep specs/ISO_COBOL.md for every remaining bare '£' and apply the same correction with the same note.
refuted.verifier: Not a reconciliation finding. The PDF and specs/ISO_COBOL.md agree character-for-character: both print '£' as the left-hand operator on the four UNSIGNED rows of the 13.18.60.4 GR-12 minimum-range table, and both print '<' on the four SIGNED rows. The transcription is faithful, so there is nothing to reconcile and the 'ocr-error' classification is incorrect. Two supporting assertions in the claim are also wrong: (a) it is NOT a recurring pattern - '£' appears exactly 4 times in the whole markdown, all on this page, and '≤' appears 0 times; (b) the Symbol-font-0xA3 etiology is unsupported - page 537 uses only Cambria (Identity-H subsets) and ArialNarrow, with obfuscated CIDs U+03B4 ('<') and U+0349 ('£'). The one true kernel is a defect in ISO's published PDF: '0 £ n < 256' is unreadable and the intended relation is '0 <= n < 2**8' (the SIGNED rows' '<' is correct as printed, since '-128 < n < 128' deliberately states a -127..127 minimum so one's-complement and sign-magnitude machines conform). Record that in the ISO-defect register with an in-place editorial note; do not alter the transcription, which would break its fidelity to the canonical source.

The claim is filed as kind=missing-heading, but all three headings are present, verbatim, with the exact printed clause numbers and titles. (2) THERE IS NOTHING IN THE PDF TO LOSE. Markdown heading depth has no counterpart in the printed page. ISO/IEC 1989:2023 sets every clause heading in the same bold face at the same size regardless of depth — on the render, '8.8.4.12.2', '8.8.4.12.3' and '8.8.4.12.4' are typographically identical, and nothing on the page typographically distinguishes a fourth-level from a fifth-level clause. The printed hierarchy is carried SOLELY by the dotted decimal number, and that number is transcribed correctly in every case. So the markdown reproduces 100% of the depth information the source actually encodes. (3) THE HIERARCHY IS PRESERVED TWICE OVER, AND ANCHOR NAVIGATION IS DEMONSTRABLY INTACT. Each heading is preceded by an explicit '' / '-3' / '-4' anchor derived from the clause number, not from heading depth (verified at :10127, :10141, :10148). The claim's assertion that 'section-anchor navigation ... will mis-parent these rules' is simply false — the anchors are correct and are unaffected by '#' count. (4) IT IS PAGE-BREAK FURNITURE, AND THE CLAIMED CONVENTION DOES NOT EXIST. I tabulated markdown level against ISO dotted depth for every numbered heading in the file. The actual mechanism is page-local: of the 594 numbered headings that open a page, 521 are '##' regardless of depth, and the remaining headings on that page are then offset relative to that page's baseline. p229 opens with depth-4 8.8.4.8 at '##' and puts depth-5 8.8.4.8.1/.2/.3 at '###' — internally consistent. p232's 8.8.4.12 is not page-opening so it kept '###'/'####'. p233 opens with a depth-5 heading, so it and its two siblings all take '##'. The claimed consequence is also not a p233-specific regression: '## Page 233' is itself a level-2 heading, so every one of the ~1,500 page markers in this file already sits as a peer of '## 8 Language fundamentals'.
